title: A rechargeable air-breathing battery with aviation-relevant specific energy

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a rechargeable battery that takes oxygen from ambient air and delivers enough electrical energy per unit of total battery mass to expand the practical possibilities of electric aviation. Its defining capability combines high delivered specific energy with useful power, repeated rechargeability and transport-appropriate safety. The accounting must include the electrolyte, oxygen-accessible electrode, housing and, for aircraft-level claims, the equipment needed to supply and manage air.

Lithium–oxygen chemistry provides a documented route toward this goal: lithium reacts with oxygen during discharge, and charging reverses the reaction. Kondori and colleagues' 2023 laboratory design used a solid electrolyte and formed predominantly lithium oxide, Li2O. Its four-electron oxygen reaction offers a chemical basis for high theoretical energy storage, but achieving that reaction reversibly is more difficult than achieving the one- and two-electron pathways discussed in the paper's abstract.

The practical concept requires these reactions to work while breathing ordinary air, with its variable moisture and other constituents, and while retaining the mass advantage after the complete device is counted. A solid electrolyte or lithium-metal electrode can contribute to that design; neither feature alone demonstrates the proposed ambient-air capability.

significance.text: As a conditional assessment, a large increase in delivered battery energy per unit mass could expand aircraft range, payload or mission options where battery mass is a binding constraint. A rechargeable air-breathing battery would be revolutionary if its chemical energy advantage survived practical construction and operation. Long-range electric flight is a possible downstream consequence, dependent on the aircraft and mission; it does not follow automatically from a high cell-level energy figure.

The gasoline analogy needs a precise boundary. The 2023 abstract describes gasoline-comparable energy density as a theoretical possibility associated with Li2O formation. It does not report that performance for a measured cell, pack or aircraft system. That comparison therefore motivates the research but cannot establish equivalent aircraft range, useful delivered energy or installed propulsion-system mass.

Aviation impact would additionally depend on sustained and peak power, charging losses, service life, safety, air handling, environmental operation, aircraft integration and certification. These are proposed practical boundaries for assessing the innovation. A laboratory report of 1,000 cycles addresses one important dimension, but cannot by itself establish an aircraft battery or predict commercial viability.

missing_breakthrough.text: The capability to establish is the simultaneous achievement of practical ambient-air operation, substantially elevated delivered specific energy, useful power, durable rechargeability and transport-appropriate safety in a fully accounted device. The supplied evidence demonstrates relevant laboratory chemistry and cycling, but does not establish this combined capability. Because the record contains no contemporary field assessment, it also cannot determine whether that combination remains unachieved as of November 1, 2026.

The chemical barrier is to sustain reversible lithium–oxygen reactions without progressively consuming active lithium or damaging the electrolyte and electrode. The reported Li2O pathway requires a difficult four-electron reaction. The abstract attributes its operation to a discharge product that conducts both ions and electrons and to that product's interface with air. Translating this mechanism into a practical device requires preserving those reaction and transport pathways over repeated operation.

The oxygen electrode must remain sufficiently porous for oxygen to reach the reacting material over many cycles. Atmospheric exposure adds chemical complications: the supplied reporting identifies water vapor as capable of causing reactions that permanently trap lithium at the electrode. CO2 tolerance is an additional proposed requirement for ordinary-air operation; the retained evidence does not demonstrate it or establish a specific CO2-related failure mechanism for this design.

Engineering synthesis: the chemical advantage must survive the mass and energy costs of electrolyte, electrode supports, housing, air treatment or circulation, controls and other necessary hardware. Practical demonstrations must also connect energy delivery to power demand, thermal behavior and safety. These requirements explain why an encouraging reaction mechanism or cycle count can leave the central system capability unresolved.

current_state.text: Kondori and colleagues reported their solid-state lithium-air battery in Science 379, pages 499–505, on February 3, 2023. The supplied review of the PubMed abstract supports room-temperature operation, Li2O as the main discharge product, rechargeability over 1,000 laboratory cycles, a low polarization gap and high-rate operation. The abstract does not provide numerical rate or polarization values in the retained evidence, and these descriptions do not establish practical cell size, aircraft power delivery or complete system performance.

John Timmer's February 6, 2023 Ars Technica article attributes an estimate of approximately 685 Wh/kg to the researchers. This preserves a potentially important quantitative result, but it remains a reported researcher estimate rather than independently validated performance in this record. The supplied evidence does not establish its mass denominator, including whether it accounts for a complete cell or pack. The number is absent from the PubMed abstract, so it cannot support a direct comparison with fully assembled lithium-ion packs without further information.

The abstract's gasoline-comparable energy statement is theoretical and separate from both the cycling result and the approximately 685 Wh/kg estimate. The retained material does not establish that the reported cycling occurred under untreated ambient air with specified humidity and CO2, nor does it establish full-cell mass accounting or transport safety. These are limits on what the supplied evidence demonstrates, not evidence that the reported laboratory result is false.

The supplied research attributes ambient-air wording and a theoretical gasoline comparison to an Argonne highlight dated February 2, 2023. No retained Argonne text was available to the review, so those attributions cannot resolve the experimental gas conditions. An alternative PDF resolved to an OSTI address, but its extraction contained no substantive text. Consequently, the review could not confirm that document's identity from its content or assess full-paper figures, experimental conditions and mass accounting. This extraction failure does not establish that the full Science paper itself was inaccessible.

The evidence summarized here concerns a dated 2023 laboratory report. The supplied record contains no freshness search establishing subsequent progress through November 1, 2026. It therefore supports the reported achievement and its stated limitations, while leaving the present field-wide availability of a practical aviation-relevant air-breathing battery unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independently built cells of a declared practical size should operate on specified ambient air and deliver specific energy several times that of a dated, explicitly identified lithium-ion pack baseline, while retaining useful performance for hundreds of cycles. These are proposed benchmarks, not established standards or aviation certification thresholds. A cell-to-pack comparison should be labeled explicitly, and any claim of a pack-level advantage should include the necessary pack and air-management equipment.
completion_criteria.label: Cells demonstrate severalfold baseline specific energy and hundreds of useful cycles

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement protocol: publish delivered electrical energy, complete cell mass, component masses, discharge rate, temperature, depth of discharge, charging conditions, capacity retention and charge–discharge energy efficiency. State the mass convention and whether it includes oxygen-containing discharge products, and identify every excluded component. Report power and energy under the same defined operating conditions so that high specific energy is not inferred from a test that leaves mission-relevant power unresolved.
completion_criteria.label: Report complete mass accounting and matched-condition energy and power

completion_criteria.text: Proposed environmental validation: disclose oxygen concentration, humidity, CO2 concentration, air flow and any purification, drying or conditioning. Test ordinary-air operation across a declared range of conditions and include the mass and energy costs of any required treatment. Water-vapor exposure is motivated by the documented risk of lithium becoming trapped through unwanted electrode reactions; CO2 testing is an additional proposed criterion whose successful performance is not established by the supplied sources.
completion_criteria.label: Validate ordinary-air operation across declared conditions, including treatment costs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundary: publish construction and testing details sufficient for independent laboratories to reproduce the performance across multiple cells, with variability and failures reported. An aviation-relevant claim would then require system-level energy and power measurements, thermal and safety evaluation, and a defined aircraft mission assessment. Successful finite tests would establish performance within the tested envelope; they would not establish operation under every atmospheric condition or suitability for every aircraft.
completion_criteria.label: Publish reproducible multicell performance with variability and practical claim boundaries

related_concepts.text: The demonstrated design overlaps solid-state electrolytes and lithium-metal batteries: the supplied reporting describes a solid electrolyte, a lithium-metal electrode and an oxygen-reacting electrode in the same device. These are compatible design features. The distinguishing target of CHEMREV-08 is the complete rechargeable ambient-air capability at high delivered specific energy; adopting a solid electrolyte or lithium metal does not alone establish that target.

Roster synthesis: CHEMREV-01, predicting realistic chemical outcomes before experiment, could assist the search for compatible electrolytes and unwanted reaction pathways. CHEMREV-05, enzyme-level catalysts on request, overlaps the need to control oxygen reactions. CHEMREV-09, phase-pure synthesis of designed crystalline solids, could contribute to reproducible electrolyte or electrode materials. Each targets a broader enabling capability; CHEMREV-08 could succeed through specialized materials and chemistry without achieving any of those general capabilities.

Roster synthesis: CHEMREV-07, fossil-competitive multicarbon chemicals from CO2 and water, shares the ambition of changing energy-related chemistry but concerns chemical production rather than rechargeable electrical storage. CHEMREV-06, mild nitrogen fixation, and CHEMREV-12, selective methane-to-methanol conversion, likewise share challenges in reaction control and practical process performance while involving different reactions, products and completion tests.

Roster synthesis: CHEMREV-03, an ambient-pressure room-temperature superconductor, could affect electrical equipment, but it would not establish a battery's electrochemical energy storage or ambient-air operation. CHEMREV-04, arbitrary stable-molecule synthesis; CHEMREV-10, atomically specified manufacture; and CHEMREV-11, selective unactivated C–H functionalization, concern forms of manufacturing control that might aid materials development without being prerequisites for this battery. CHEMREV-02, synthetic Darwinian evolution, and CHEMREV-13, plastics returned economically to monomers, have no direct enabling relationship established by the supplied material. All remain distinct entries.

unresolved_issues: Whether subsequent work has demonstrated the combined practical capability by November 1, 2026; no freshness search was supplied.
The mass denominator, operating conditions and measurement basis underlying the approximately 685 Wh/kg researcher estimate.
The full experimental conditions behind the 1,000-cycle result, including cell size, cycling depth, retention, numerical rates, polarization and gas composition.
Whether untreated ambient-air operation, humidity tolerance and CO2 tolerance were demonstrated under defined conditions.
The unverified Argonne wording and the identity and substantive contents of the alternative OSTI PDF.
A dated lithium-ion comparison baseline and precise practical size, energy, power, life and safety targets for the proposed completion test.
The installed-system mass, air-management burden and aircraft mission envelope needed to translate cell performance into aviation capability.

brief.title: A rechargeable battery that breathes air to power flight
possible: Electric aircraft could fly farther or carry more cargo with a battery that delivers much more energy for its weight. It would draw oxygen from ordinary air, recharge repeatedly and supply the power needed for flight.
why: Battery weight limits what electric aircraft can do. More usable energy for the same weight would give aircraft designers more room to trade between range, payload and different missions.

sources.showed: Their laboratory battery used a solid electrolyte, the material that carries charged atoms between its reacting surfaces. It operated at room temperature and mainly formed lithium oxide, a compound of lithium and oxygen.
sources.quote: The battery is rechargeable for 1000 cycles with a low polarization gap and can operate at high rates.
sources.cited_for: The work demonstrates rechargeable lithium–oxygen chemistry with a solid electrolyte.
sources.not_established: It does not establish a complete battery that combines ordinary-air operation, low weight, flight power and transport safety.

sources.showed: This research highlight describes the battery using ambient-air language and a theoretical comparison with gasoline.
sources.cited_for: It describes the proposed connection between air-breathing chemistry and high energy storage.
sources.not_established: The theoretical gasoline comparison does not establish measured battery energy or aircraft range.

sources.showed: The researchers estimated energy storage of about 685 watt-hours per kilogram, a measure of energy for a given weight. The report also explains how moisture can trap lithium in unwanted reactions.
sources.quote: The researchers estimate that, even in this immature state, the technology stored about 685 watt-hours per kilogram, which is more than double most current batteries.
sources.cited_for: The report supplies the researchers’ energy estimate and explains a barrier to operation in ordinary air.
sources.not_established: The estimate does not establish an advantage after all battery components and air-handling equipment are weighed.

shown: Kondori and colleagues reported a laboratory battery that recharged for 1,000 cycles. This demonstrates repeated operation of the chemistry; it leaves the combined demands of a practical aircraft battery unresolved.
missing: A practical battery still needs to combine high energy for its total weight, useful power, repeated charging and transport safety.
Ordinary-air operation needs testing across changes in moisture and carbon dioxide, including any air-treatment burden.
The weight advantage needs to survive the housing, controls and equipment needed to supply and manage air.
Independent laboratories need to reproduce performance across multiple cells and report failures and variation.

milestones.label: Practical cells deliver more energy and lasting performance
milestones.explanation: Independently built cells of stated practical size would have to deliver several times a named lithium-ion pack’s energy per weight on specified ambient air for hundreds of useful cycles. This would test the core advantage.

milestones.label: Complete weight accounting supports matched energy and power measurements
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to report delivered energy and power under matched conditions, component weights, exclusions, charging losses and retained capacity. This would reveal whether the weight advantage holds at useful power.

milestones.label: Ordinary-air performance survives changing conditions and treatment costs
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to demonstrate operation across stated oxygen, moisture, carbon dioxide and airflow conditions, counting air-treatment weight and energy. This would test whether ordinary air preserves the advantage.

milestones.label: Reproducible results support a defined aircraft mission
milestones.explanation: Detailed methods would have to enable independent reproduction across cells, with variation and failures reported. System energy, power, heat, safety and mission tests would then define the aircraft uses the results support.

uncertain: Which components and operating conditions underlie the reported energy-per-weight estimate remains unclear.
The ordinary-air conditions, cell size and depth of discharge behind the cycling result remain unresolved.
The practical size, comparison battery and energy, power, lifetime and safety targets for judging success still need definition.

page.title: Rechargeable air-breathing lithium–air battery modules
page.definition: A rechargeable lithium–air battery module obtains its oxygen reactant from ambient air and delivers electrical energy at more than 1,000 Wh/kg and 1,000 Wh/L. Its mass and volume include the equipment needed to supply and condition that air.

goal.need: NASA's 2018 aviation diagram placed general aviation at 400 Wh/kg and regional jets at 750 Wh/kg, against a 180 Wh/kg lithium-ion reference. These aircraft-design estimates motivate batteries that deliver more electrical energy per unit mass. The diagram does not specify a cell or pack mass boundary.

figures.caption: Specific-energy reference points in NASA's 2018 aviation diagram
figures.note: Historical design estimates, not certification requirements; the cell/pack mass boundary is unspecified.

completion.title: A rechargeable 1 kWh air-breathing module exceeds 1,000 Wh/kg and 1,000 Wh/L.
completion.criterion: Demonstrate a module delivering at least 1 kWh from ambient air, with electrical discharge energy exceeding 1,000 Wh/kg and 1,000 Wh/L. Electrically recharge and discharge the same assembled module again. Include the complete module and necessary air-supply and air-conditioning equipment in both denominators, using maximum operating mass and volume, including absorbed oxygen. Air conditioning is permitted. This combines ARPA-E's published module targets with an explicitly defined air-breathing boundary.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis; ARPA-E published the numerical targets for IIT's solid-state lithium–air module, but did not publish this combined ambient-air test.
completion.basis: Searched NASA lithium–air aviation objectives, ARPA-E PROPEL-1K/JOULES-1K targets, and FAA/EASA lithium–air certification criteria. No published test combined ambient-air operation, complete air-system accounting, module energy, cycling, power and safety. This narrower demonstration uses ARPA-E's 1 kWh module target and electrical rechargeability; it does not establish aircraft qualification or a service-life requirement.

milestones.title: Analytical and laboratory tests demonstrate a rechargeable lithium–oxygen cell.
milestones.criterion: Analytical and laboratory studies demonstrate the lithium–oxygen discharge/recharge function, applying NASA's generic TRL 3 proof-of-concept criterion. Kondori et al. reported room-temperature Li₂O formation and 1,000 laboratory cycles on 3 February 2023; the abstract gives no replicate count. NIMS's assessment dated 19 September 2025 identifies capacity-limited cycling at 1,000 mAh/g of catalyst, which does not demonstrate module specific energy.
milestones.set_by: NASA, Technology Readiness Levels, TRL 3; its generic maturity criterion is applied to lithium–oxygen chemistry without assigning an official NASA rating.
milestones.threshold_quote: Generally both analytical and laboratory studies are required at this level

milestones.title: Lithium–air chemistry demonstrates at least 1,000 Wh/kg and 1,000 Wh/L.
milestones.criterion: Experimentally demonstrate both ≥1,000 Wh/kg and ≥1,000 Wh/L at chemistry level, the PROPEL-1K Phase 1 target. Ko et al., published on 17 June 2026, report 1,032 Wh/kg and 374 W/kg from a coin-size Li–O₂ cell at 60 °C, 3 mA/cm² and 8.25 mAh/cm², calculated from listed component masses; the main text gives no high-energy replicate count. This does not establish the volumetric target or air-fed module performance. ARPA-E's 2026 IIT description records Phase 1 validation without numerical test data.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-E, PROPEL-1K Phase 1 deliverables, recapped in its annual-meeting presentation dated 15 July 2025; the programme FAQ defines the two 1K energy-density units.
milestones.threshold_quote: Experimentally Show 1K performance at the Chemistry level.

milestones.title: A 1 kWh lithium–air prototype reaches 700 Wh/kg and 700 Wh/L with its supporting equipment.
milestones.criterion: Construct a packaged benchtop lithium–air energy-storage prototype of at least 1 kWh and meet ARPA-E's Phase Two size-dependent prototype thresholds. At 1 kWh these are ≥700 Wh/kg and ≥700 Wh/L; the published examples rise to 800 at 10 kWh, 900 at 100 kWh and 1,000 at 1 MWh. The clarification explicitly allows for supporting equipment, termed balance of plant.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-E, PROPEL-1K annual-meeting presentation dated 15 July 2025, slides 17–18; both thresholds are stated in the slide 17 table.

not_found: No public test report meeting the combined completion criterion was found in searches of ARPA-E, IIT, Air Energy and recent lithium–oxygen papers through 14 November 2026.
The JOULES-1K IIT project description gives no numerical cycle-life, discharge-power or gas-composition requirement, or complete installed-system mass boundary.
The Argonne CNM highlight and Science full text returned HTTP 403; the NSF-hosted manuscript timed out.
